sections.heading: Asking you to guard me from the traps around me and in me
sections.text:
Blessed God, there are more traps around me and inside me than I can even see. Please protect me.

When laziness starts to take over, lift my eyes to the life you have promised. When people draw me toward sin, make those ways taste bitter to me. When bodily pleasures pull at me in the wrong direction, cleanse my desires and make them whole. When I start wanting more and more of what this world can give, teach me to be rich toward you. When empty things look attractive, keep me from rushing into fresh guilt and damage.
theological_themes: Human beings face temptation both from outside pressures and inward desires, and need God’s active protection.
The prayer asks not only for avoidance of sin, but for reordered desires: to hate what destroys and love what leads to God.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches his disciples to ask the Father for deliverance from temptation and evil, which directly grounds this request for protection from snares both inward and outward.

John warns that disordered desire for the world is passing away, while doing God’s will endures. That supports the prayer’s concern about worldly possessions, vanities, and learning to desire what lasts.
Jesus’ parable of the rich fool exposes the danger of storing up earthly abundance while not being rich toward God, matching the prayer’s request to value God above possessions.

sections.heading: Remembering the freedom you have given me
sections.text:
Help me remember what it means that you have set me free. Don’t let me become so busy that I stop caring for my soul. Don’t let the urgent things of this life crowd out the eternal things that matter most.

I don’t want merely to get through life. I want to grow toward you.
theological_themes: Redemption gives the believer a new dignity and a new responsibility to live as one who belongs to God.
The prayer asks for eternal-mindedness without despising ordinary life, refusing to let temporary concerns eclipse communion with God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes Christian redemption as freedom secured by Christ, and calls believers not to return to bondage. This illuminates the prayer’s language of spiritual release and living in a manner worthy of it.
Paul calls believers united to the risen Christ to set their minds on things above. That supports the prayer’s desire not to be so absorbed in time that eternity is neglected.

sections.heading: Learning to understand grace rightly
sections.text:
Shape the way I think about life with you. Keep me from misunderstanding your grace. Don’t let me judge my spiritual health by the wrong standards, or confuse real growth with the energy, personality, discipline, or effort I can produce on my own.

Teach me to see your work as your work, and to depend on you while I obey.
theological_themes: Grace must be understood according to God’s gospel, not by natural self-effort or merely human measures of progress.
Christian growth involves real obedience, but it is rooted in God’s gracious work rather than self-generated spirituality.

scripture_references.connection: Paul holds together salvation by grace, not works, with believers being created in Christ for good works. This grounds the prayer’s distinction between grace and merely natural effort.
Paul rebukes believers for trying to complete by the flesh what began by the Spirit. That directly supports the request not to measure spiritual advance by unaided human effort.

sections.heading: Asking for a life that pleases you everywhere
sections.text:
Increase my love for you. Make me willing to yield myself fully to your will. Grow in me a wide and practical love for other people.

Give me patience when life is hard, and courage that does not collapse under pressure. Make my heart more at home with you than with this world. And let me care deeply about pleasing you—not only where people can see me, but also when no one is watching.
theological_themes: The believer seeks deeper love for God, surrendered obedience, love for neighbor, endurance, and integrity before God in public and private.
Holiness is not confined to visible religious activity; it includes hidden motives, ordinary conduct, and perseverance under trial.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers, in view of God’s mercy, to offer themselves to God and be transformed rather than conformed to the world. This supports the prayer’s surrender, renewed desires, and concern to please God.

Paul prays that believers would know God’s will, walk in a manner pleasing to him, bear fruit, and be strengthened with endurance. These themes closely match the prayer’s requests for obedience, patience, and spiritual fruitfulness.
Jesus warns against performing righteousness for human approval and teaches secret devotion before the Father. This supports the prayer’s desire to please God both publicly and privately.

sections.heading: Make me look more like Christ
sections.text:
Draw the likeness of Jesus onto my soul—every line, every feature, every part of me that you are making new. Make me someone in whom you take delight, not because I have made myself impressive, but because I am your workmanship in Christ.

Write your truth into my life by your Spirit. Break up the hard ground in me, plant what you want to grow, and bring a harvest that belongs to you.
theological_themes: Sanctification is God’s creative work, conforming the believer to Christ by the Holy Spirit.
The images of workmanship, Spirit-written letter, and cultivated soil emphasize that the believer’s fruitfulness comes from God’s action and is meant for God’s pleasure.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says believers are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works. This directly grounds the prayer’s request that God form Christlike fruit in the believer.
Paul describes believers as a letter from Christ written by the Spirit of the living God. This supports the image of God writing his life and truth into the believer by the Spirit.
Paul describes the fruit produced by the Spirit, showing that Christlike character is not self-manufactured but grown by God’s Spirit in the believer.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The phrase “When sinners entice me” could be misunderstood as contempt for unbelievers; it has been rendered as resistance to being drawn toward sinful ways, not withdrawal from or superiority over other people.

The original’s contrast between grace and “the efforts of my natural being” could sound as if the body or human effort itself is evil. It has been interpreted as a warning against measuring sanctification by unaided human strength, temperament, or self-generated spirituality.
The prayer’s strong language about guilt and ruin has been retained in contemporary terms, because the original treats sin as spiritually destructive rather than merely unhelpful or unhealthy.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Views of heaven” was rendered as having one’s eyes lifted to the life God has promised, preserving the eternal perspective without making the prayer sound escapist.
“Right notions of religion” was interpreted as a true understanding of life with God and of grace, since the original is concerned with sound spiritual judgment rather than abstract religious theory.
“Draw on my soul the lineaments of Christ” was rendered as God drawing the likeness of Jesus onto the soul, preserving the concrete image of Christ’s features being formed in the believer.

The final images—workmanship, Spirit-written letter, and tilled soil—were kept as concrete metaphors because they are central to the original’s view of sanctification as God’s active work producing visible fruit.
